how: Connected means the conflict can affect the population's lives through that channel. A cell is marked connected only if a change has been observed in the past 12 months or at least one concrete conduit, such as a shipping route, an imported good, a troop deployment, or an organization, has been identified. A general argument alone is not enough; such cells are marked not connected.
A judgment about the strength of the evidence. For high-confidence cells, the sources were opened and checked against the evidence statement.
The data needed to decide the cell are not available. Rather than guess, each such cell states what data would make a judgment possible.

Cells in this channel identify who is behind the attack: state, non-state (criminal organizations and the like), mixed state and non-state, or unidentified. State involvement is shown only when there is evidence and a source.

The people of South Korea; the U.S.; the Nordic and Baltic states; Southern Europe; Western, Central, and Eastern Europe (including the EU's central and eastern members); and the countries involved in each conflict.

A separate reviewer, working without knowledge of the original reasoning, checked every cell against its sources and the logic of its pathway. The same conduit is judged the same way wherever it appears.
The map shows whether a pathway exists. It does not put a number on the size or likelihood of any harm.

fps.st: In the fifth year of full-scale war, Russia is pressing its offensive toward Kostiantynivka and Dobropillia while Ukraine mounts local counterattacks around Kupiansk, Chasiv Yar, and elsewhere. Every short truce—at Easter in April, on Victory Day in May, and on September 5–8—ended with a return to fighting. Washington is trying to reconvene three-way U.S.-Russia-Ukraine technical talks in the UAE, but Moscow is holding to its demand for all of the Donetsk region.

fps.n: Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
fps.st: The war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, is now in its eighth month. After an April ceasefire and a June 17 memorandum of understanding effectively collapsed on July 8, the United States reimposed its naval blockade on July 14. In Hormuz, Iran is trying to control passage by attacking merchant ships and laying mines, while the U.S. military escorts transits; U.S. Central Command said it had turned back 144 merchant vessels between resuming the blockade and October 31. Ship-tracking data and U.S. government statements diverge sharply on how much traffic is getting through. Ship-tracking data in early September showed between five and 12 vessels a day, roughly 10 percent of the peacetime level of about 100. Yet U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on September 28 that about 13 million barrels a day were passing through, and the ship-tracking firm Kpler counted 19 tankers transiting in the week to September 27. On September 25, Iran put forward a roadmap for reopening the strait within seven days, but President Trump rejected it on September 26. On the nuclear front, Natanz and other sites have been destroyed again, but about 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent has been beyond IAEA verification since June 2025.
fps.pt: Iran, Israel, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, United States

fps.st: The Israel-Hezbollah war, which reignited in March alongside the Iran war, has left Israeli forces occupying about 55 villages south of the Litani River, and fighting continues under a nominal ceasefire. In Gaza, an agreement on the phased disarmament of Hamas was announced on July 31, but whether Israel will formally accept and implement it remains unclear.

The peace treaty initialed at the White House in August 2025 remains unsigned because Armenia has not first amended its constitution, as Azerbaijan demands. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan's ruling party won the June parliamentary elections but fell short of the seats needed to change the constitution. Construction has yet to begin on the 43-kilometer Meghri section of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), for which only about $400 million in initial U.S. funding has been secured, while Turkey and Azerbaijan are pursuing a parallel Kars-Dilucu railway that bypasses Armenia.

Under Ahmed al-Sharaa's transitional government, Syria has entered a phase of integration and reconstruction: in August the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) disbanded and merged into the government army, and the United States lifted Syria's designation as a state sponsor of terrorism. Tensions persist, however, as Israel keeps troops in the south and in August struck as far afield as an air base in Idlib. Much depends on whether U.S.-mediated de-escalation talks between Israel and Syria bear fruit.

Ukraine is repeatedly striking Novorossiysk, the Black Sea Fleet's new base, and tankers of Russia's shadow fleet with drones, Neptune missiles, and uncrewed surface vessels. The fleet has effectively been pushed out of Sevastopol, and with even Russia's crude export ports now within Ukraine's reach, the risks to Russian seaborne logistics have grown.

Since the Justice Mission-2025 encirclement drills in December 2025, no named large-scale exercise by the People's Liberation Army (PLA) had been confirmed through September 2026, and Chinese military aircraft entered Taiwan's air defense identification zone (ADIZ) 125 times in August, less than half the monthly average for 2024–25. Gray-zone pressure, however, has become routine, from coast guard incursions around Kinmen and Dongsha (Pratas) to the announced integration of Kinmen and Xiamen. Amid U.S.-China summitry, Trump has treated arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip and Taiwan's Legislative Yuan has cut the defense budget, eroding the political foundations of deterrence.

At its Ninth Party Congress, North Korea designated South Korea a permanently hostile state and severed inter-Korean links, and its ballistic missile launches have surged in 2026 to nine rounds involving 15 or more missiles. Trump, pursuing a meeting with Kim Jong Un before the end of the year, unilaterally scaled back the joint South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise. Seoul has floated a plan to trade a nuclear freeze for sanctions relief, but Pyongyang rejects denuclearization as an agenda item altogether. The expanding deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, now including drone operators, is fueling concern that Moscow will pay Pyongyang back with military technology.

For 11 months since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's remarks on a Taiwan contingency in November 2025, China has maintained a ban on exports of dual-use items and rare earths to Japan, a halt to imports of Japanese seafood, and curbs on travel to Japan. Military pressure has continued as well—fire-control radar lock-ons by fighter jets, live-fire drills near Okinotori, and joint Chinese-Russian bomber flights—and leader-level channels are effectively frozen. Japan is responding by building up its defenses and deepening cooperation with Australia and other partners.

After spending a record number of days in the waters contiguous to the Senkakus in 2025, the China Coast Guard has continued to enter the islands' territorial waters repeatedly in 2026. On June 10 and July 7, the two countries' coast guards faced off in territorial waters around Japanese fishing boats, sharpening a contest over who enforces the law there. A deliberate armed clash is unlikely, but the risk of an accidental one is ever present.

fps.n: Structures in the Korea-China Provisional Measures Zone (PMZ), Yellow Sea
fps.st: South Korea and China have been at odds over the aquaculture facilities (Shenlan 1 and 2) and a management platform that China installed in the PMZ. After the January summit in Beijing between Lee Jae-myung and Xi Jinping, China moved and dismantled the management platform, which the South Korean government called "meaningful progress." But the aquaculture facilities and many observation buoys remain, and cases of the China Coast Guard obstructing South Korean ocean surveys have piled up, so concerns about gray-zone encroachment have not been laid to rest.

The China Coast Guard maintains a constant presence and blocks Philippine vessels, and buoys and floating platforms apparently installed by China were spotted in late May 2026, heightening fears that artificial structures will go up on the shoal. Right after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi warned the Philippines of bitter consequences on July 22 over a clash at Second Thomas Shoal, the China Coast Guard fired water cannon at Philippine vessels near Scarborough on two consecutive days, July 23 and 24, and in late September a Philippine-led multinational exercise was held nearby.

Since a provisional arrangement in July 2024, Philippine resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre had proceeded without interference. On September 24, 2026, however, China Coast Guard vessels and three navy ships obstructed a resupply mission 60 nautical miles from the shoal, forcing it to be called off. The October 21 resupply went through without being blocked, and the China Coast Guard announced that it had taken place "with China's permission." The Philippine military countered that it had not sought permission.

New construction, including what appears to be a radar installation, has been spotted in the Paracels, which China has controlled since 1974, prompting a formal protest from Vietnam in August. Vietnam is also expanding land reclamation in the Spratlys, and the two countries are now competing to fortify the islands.

fps.n: India-Pakistan (Kashmir, the Arabian Sea, and the Indus)
fps.st: The ceasefire that ended the four-day conflict of May 2025 is holding, but India continues to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance. In late August the Court of Arbitration constituted under the treaty ruled the suspension invalid, but India does not recognize the court's jurisdiction. On September 15, warships from the two countries collided in the Arabian Sea—their first direct military contact since 2025—and with no naval hotline or incidents-at-sea agreement between them, the risk of accidental escalation is high.

Relations have been stabilizing since the 2024 agreement on troop disengagement in eastern Ladakh, and the 25th round of Special Representatives talks in August 2026 discussed which parts of the boundary delimitation could be settled first (an "early harvest"). At a meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September, Modi and Xi agreed to pursue a fair settlement of the border, but both sides' large troop deployments and China's dam on the upper Brahmaputra remain unresolved.

After clashes in July and December 2025, a ceasefire was reached in a joint statement on December 27 and is holding, but both Thailand and Cambodia call it fragile. Tensions persist over Thailand's cancellation in May of the 2001 memorandum of understanding on maritime boundaries, Cambodia's launch of UN conciliation proceedings in June, and the return of residents to the Ban Nong Chan area, and in September the Thai military warned of a full-scale response.

Min Aung Hlaing became president in April 2026 following elections, but the move is seen as having changed only the outward form of military rule. The junta has regained some of the initiative through conscription and Chinese support, and northern Shan State has stabilized under Chinese-brokered ceasefires, but fighting continues on the Kachin (Bhamo), Rakhine (Sittwe), and Karen fronts.

Since Pakistan declared open war on the Taliban government on February 27, 2026, airstrikes and border clashes have recurred, and a March airstrike on a hospital in Kabul killed more than 260 civilians. Mediation by Qatar, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and China has failed to produce a lasting ceasefire, and on September 24 Pakistan extended its airstrikes as far as Kandahar, citing a terrorist attack on a police headquarters and drone attacks launched from Afghanistan. On October 11, after a standoff between the federal and provincial governments over counterterrorism, President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency and imposed governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the province bordering Afghanistan; Parliament approved the measures for two months on October 15.

With traffic through Hormuz effectively paralyzed by the Iran war, the Strait of Malacca has become even more important strategically to Asia's energy supply chains. In April, Indonesia's finance minister floated the idea of charging transit fees, then dropped it after the Foreign Ministry objected, but the remark alone pushed up shipping insurance premiums. Piracy and armed robbery incidents in the strait are among the most numerous in Asia.

fps.n: Baltic Sea, Kaliningrad, and the Suwałki Gap
fps.st: Russian provocations on NATO's eastern flank have multiplied since the start of September. A Russian warship fired flares at a Danish helicopter (September 14), NATO shot down a drone over Lithuania (September 15), and an Mi-8 helicopter from Kaliningrad violated Polish airspace (September 23–24). Lithuania's communications regulator said in May 2026 that GPS-spoofing antennas in Kaliningrad had grown from three in early 2025 to 36, able to spoof signals within a radius of 450 kilometers. Courtroom and maritime standoffs over severed undersea cables and the crackdown on the shadow fleet also continue.
fps.pt: Russia, Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Denmark, Germany, Finland, Sweden, Belarus

fps.n: NATO's southeastern airspace (Romania and the Black Sea)
fps.st: Whenever Russia strikes southern Ukraine, drones and missiles stray across Romania's Danube border. On September 24, Romania shot down a drone suspected of being Russian, and on September 25 F-16s and Spanish F-18s were scrambled. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed intelligence that Russia is planning hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries that support Ukraine.

The Greenland crisis, set off by Trump's threats of annexation, was brought into an institutional framework on September 22, when the United States, Denmark, and Greenland concluded a security agreement. Washington gained an expansion of Pituffik and two new bases, a right of consent over any base established by a non-NATO country, and the power to screen foreign investment. Because the agreement remains in force even if Greenland becomes independent, some observers conclude that it has established de facto U.S. security sovereignty over Greenland. The risk of armed conflict has receded, but the sovereignty dispute lies dormant.
fps.pt: Denmark, GRL, United States, Norway, Canada

fps.st: In Serbia, after nearly two years of antigovernment protests, Aleksandar Vučić gave up the presidency on September 27 to run for prime minister in early elections on October 25. The Student List, however, won 52.7 percent of the vote and 140 of 250 seats (preliminary count by the electoral commission), and Vučić conceded defeat. In Bosnia's October 4 general election, Milorad Dodik's party, the SNSD, won both the presidency of Republika Srpska and the Serb seat on the three-member state presidency. Dodik was barred from running by a 2025 conviction. The question of Serbs in northern Kosovo remains unresolved.

fps.n: Russian and Iranian hybrid attacks (Germany and the U.K.)
fps.st: After explosive-laden drones, apparently targeting transport aircraft bound for Ukraine, were found near Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, Germany on September 1 formally named Russia as the culprit for the first time. Britain summoned Russian diplomats, and it emerged that Iran-linked hackers had knocked a British power plant offline for four days. At sea, a Russian frigate fired warning shots near a British yacht south of the Isle of Wight on June 16. Britain's Ministry of Defence said the shots were not aimed at the vessel and treated the episode as an isolated incident.
fps.pt: Germany, United Kingdom, Russia, Iran, Poland

fps.n: Regime change in Venezuela under U.S. pressure
fps.st: After U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro on January 3, Washington recognized Delcy Rodríguez's interim government and set up an arrangement under which it effectively oversees Venezuela's oil sector. Armed conflict has subsided, but no election timetable has been set, the apparatus of repression remains in place, and the damage from a major earthquake in June has compounded matters, leaving the transition unstable.

fps.n: Strikes on drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific (Operation Southern Spear)
fps.st: U.S. military strikes on vessels suspected of carrying drugs, which began in September 2025, have continued for more than a year, and the cumulative death toll has passed 230. The campaign has expanded to strikes on land in Venezuela and Ecuador, and because the United States has not released its evidence, it continues to draw charges of extrajudicial killing.

Since January the United States has been intercepting tankers bound for Cuba and threatening tariffs on countries that supply it with fuel, plunging the island into a humanitarian crisis marked by fuel shortages, the collapse of the power grid, and rising infant mortality. The Trump administration has named Cuba as the next target for regime change and keeps adding sanctions, while talks between the two countries drag on without result.

Trump has vowed land strikes on the cartels, but no U.S. military strike on Mexican territory has been confirmed to date, and Mexico has eased the pressure for U.S. military intervention by killing El Mencho and carrying out large-scale extraditions. The border is being militarized, with U.S. forces shooting down cartel drones with lasers, and Mexico has stayed out of the Shield of the Americas.

After Panama's Supreme Court in January struck down as unconstitutional CK Hutchison's concession to operate the ports of Balboa and Cristóbal, Denmark's Maersk and MSC took over interim operations. China retaliated with inspections of Panama-flagged ships and stricter customs checks on agricultural products, and the sale of CK Hutchison's ports business to a BlackRock consortium is held up by a Chinese antitrust review.

With the Transitional Presidential Council dissolved in February, Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé governs alone, while gangs control most of Port-au-Prince and about 1.5 million people are internally displaced. The UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force (GSF) has deployed about 1,500 of its authorized 5,550 personnel, and on September 29 the UN Security Council extended its mandate by six months, to March 31, 2027 (China, Russia, and Pakistan abstained). On December 13, Haiti is scheduled to hold its first elections since 2016.

After talks broke down in late August, the United States imposed 50 percent tariffs and Canada retaliated with tariffs on about $20 billion worth of goods, turning the dispute into an all-out trade war between allies. Washington escalated with a ban on imports of Canadian dairy products and alcohol (effective September 29) and exclusion from government procurement, and an October 19 referendum related to Alberta's separation adds to the tension.

fps.n: Ecuador: gang violence and joint operations with U.S. forces
fps.st: With the homicide rate at about 49 per 100,000 people, President Daniel Noboa's government again declared a 60-day state of emergency in September. Since March it has conducted ground strikes alongside the U.S. military near the Colombian border, drawing controversy over errant strikes, while a proposal to allow foreign military bases was rejected in a 2025 referendum.

Since the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) captured El Fasher in October 2025, the front has shifted to Kordofan, where El Obeid is under siege, and to Blue Nile. The war is spilling across borders: the army has struck RSF convoys inside Chad with drones, and RSF drones are alleged to be launching from Ethiopian territory. Five-way mediation by the AU, the EU, IGAD, the Arab League, and the UN has made no progress.
fps.pt: Sudan, TCD, Ethiopia, United Arab Emirates, Egypt

fps.n: Sahel jihadist insurgency (Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger)
fps.st: JNIM has been blockading fuel supply routes into Mali's capital, Bamako, for a year, and in April a joint offensive by JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) drove government forces and Russia's Africa Corps out of the north. In Niger, an attempted coup on August 29 was put down with Russian and Algerian support, while mutual assistance within the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) failed to work.
fps.pt: Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Russia, Algeria

fps.n: Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (M23 and Rwanda)
fps.st: After M23 seized Goma and Bukavu in 2025, the Washington Accords (DRC-Rwanda) and the Doha Framework (DRC-M23) followed, but implementation has been slow. Despite an August negotiating roadmap and the deployment of ceasefire monitors, government-aligned forces launched offensives toward Minembwe and Walungu, and an Ebola outbreak has deepened the humanitarian crisis.
fps.pt: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, BDI, Qatar, United States

fps.n: Horn of Africa (Tigray war and Ethiopia-Eritrea)
fps.st: On September 22, full-scale war broke out in Tigray, Amhara, and Afar between Ethiopian government forces and an antigovernment coalition including the TPLF and Fano militias, effectively bringing down the order established by the Pretoria agreement. The Ethiopian government accuses Eritrea of aiding the rebels, and that charge, coupled with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's demand for an outlet to the Red Sea (the port of Assab), has raised the risk of war between Ethiopia and Eritrea.

fps.n: Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb (Houthis and Yemen's civil war)
fps.st: Alongside the Iran war, the Houthis have stepped up attacks aimed at Saudi Arabia, and with Yemen's civil war reignited they have seized the port of Mocha and Perim Island. The Houthis say they will target only Saudi vessels, but the risks to shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have grown, and Saudi Arabia's crude export route, rerouted to the Red Sea to avoid Hormuz, is under threat as well.
fps.pt: Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Eritrea, DJI

fps.st: With the Hormuz blockade diverting Saudi crude through the East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea, and ships heading north through Suez to escape the Houthi threat, the canal's traffic and toll revenue have rebounded. Transits reached 1,340 in July, up 27 percent from a year earlier, and 2026 revenue is projected at $5.8 billion to $6 billion. Egyptian ports themselves have come under threat, however, as the drone attack on the port of Damietta showed.

Amid the standoff between the Government of National Unity in Tripoli and Khalifa Haftar's forces in the east, a UN-brokered roadmap for unified elections within 24 months was signed on August 30. It needs the approval of the House of Representatives and the High Council of State within a month, and sources of instability remain, including the assassination of the Libyan National Army (LNA) intelligence chief in August and a drone attack on the Zawiya refinery.

When Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025, Somalia reacted in January 2026 by cancelling all its agreements with the UAE. Armed clashes have broken out in Mogadishu over the extension of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term, while Puntland and Jubaland are moving to break away and al-Shabaab is expanding its reach.
fps.pt: Somalia, Israel, United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia

fps.n: U.S.-China chip rivalry and Korean fabs in China
fps.st: At the end of 2025, the United States revoked the validated end-user (VEU) status of Samsung's Xi'an plant and SK hynix's plants in Wuxi and Dalian, issuing equipment import licenses valid only for 2026. The licenses prohibit expansion and upgrades, but the process transitions the two companies carried out around the time the licenses were issued—236-layer NAND at Xi'an and DDR5 at Wuxi—could become a point of contention when the licenses come up for renewal for 2027. With State Council Decree No. 835 (April 2026), China created a legal basis for sanctioning companies that comply with U.S. controls. The U.S.-China summit in September extended the tariff truce to January 10, 2027, but chip controls were not on the agenda.
fps.pt: South Korea, United States, China, Taiwan, Japan, Netherlands

fps.st: A frozen conflict with no fighting, Transnistria has hosted Russian troops since the 1992 ceasefire. The Russia-Ukraine War analysis holds that a ceasefire can hold for long only if great-power forces stand on the dividing line, and Transnistria is one of its precedents. Whether the Russian troops here stay or go is therefore a signal that tests that assessment. In April 2026, Moldova's General Inspectorate for Migration designated foreigners, including commanders of the Operational Group of Russian Forces, as barred from entering or residing in Moldova. In May, a Russian presidential decree (No. 330) eased the requirements for the region's residents to obtain Russian citizenship. In August, Moldova's intelligence and security authorities estimated the stockpile at the Cobasna ammunition depot at about 14,000 tons gross weight, with a net explosive content of about 2,800 tons. Gas for the region is bought on European spot markets with Russian money, and Moldova has raised its gas reserve requirement for the region to 135.9 million cubic meters, to be met by November 1.

cells.m: Deepening military cooperation between Russia and North Korea → North Korean troops gain combat experience and Russian technical help → The military threat on the Korean Peninsula could grow.
cells.b: South Korea's National Intelligence Service (NIS) said in early 2026 that about 11,000 North Korean troops (about 10,000 combat troops and about 1,000 engineers) were stationed in Russia's Kursk region, and that they were learning modern combat tactics, gathering battlefield data, and upgrading their weapons systems with Russian technical help (Kyiv Independent, citing Yonhap, February 13, 2026).

cells.r: The United States supplies weapons and intelligence, but U.S. forces are not a party to the fighting, so the direct military threat to Americans' daily lives is weak.

cells.m: A drawn-out war → Sustained Russian military pressure along its western borders → Tighter border security and heavier defense burdens for the Nordic and Baltic states
cells.b: On December 12, 2025, Lithuania's parliament approved a record 2026 defense budget of 4.79 billion euros (5.38 percent of GDP, up from 4.01 percent the year before). A joint investigation by Nordic and Baltic public broadcasters (June 10, 2026) found that Russia is building new barracks and depots near the Finnish border, which could raise the number of troops it can deploy there from about 20,000 to 80,000 (an estimate by the commander of the Finnish Army). NATO's Baltic commander, however, saw a low risk of direct conflict while Russia is fighting in Ukraine, warning that this could change quickly after a ceasefire. Airspace violations, including the drone shot down over Lithuania in September 2026, are covered under the Baltic Sea and Kaliningrad flashpoint.

cells.r: Southern Europe is far from the front, and no realistic direct military threat stemming from this war has been confirmed.

cells.m: Russian airstrikes on Ukrainian areas near the border → Drones entering Romanian and Polish airspace and debris falling → Danger to residents of border areas and evacuations
cells.b: According to Romanian defense authorities, there had been seven incursions by Russian drones into Romanian airspace and 11 debris finds as of April 28, 2026; on April 25, a drone fell in Galați, forcing about 200 residents to evacuate and damaging property (ABC News, May 2, 2026).

cells.m: Fighting on the front lines and long-range strikes by both sides → Civilian casualties and destruction of homes and infrastructure in both countries
cells.b: As reported on September 25, 2026, Russian strikes killed at least seven people in Kyiv, and Ukrainian drone attacks around the same time caused casualties in Russia, including in Voronezh.

cells.m: Sanctions on Russia and a drawn-out war → Uncertainty over the supply of, and payment for, the Sakhalin-2 LNG that Korea Gas Corporation imports under a long-term contract → Households could face higher gas and electricity bills.
cells.b: The EU's 19th sanctions package (October 2025) barred EU companies from providing shipping, insurance, and other services for Russian LNG bound for third countries, which could have made it hard for South Korea to import Sakhalin-2 LNG from January 2027. The 21st package, adopted on July 23, 2026, exempted Sakhalin-2 LNG bound for South Korea and Japan until March 31, 2028 (South Korea's industry ministry expects stable imports of about 2 million tons over the rest of the contract), and Britain issued an exemption license with the same deadline on October 1. Combined Sakhalin-2 imports by South Korea and Japan in 2026 come to about 4.8 million tons (5.9 percent of their total LNG). No effect on gas or electricity bills could be confirmed.

cells.r: The United States is a net energy exporter, and this channel works only through the general effect of world oil prices; no specific link to Americans has been confirmed.

cells.m: The war, sanctions on Russia, and the EU's phased ban on Russian gas imports → Gas and power price swings in Europe's integrated market → Nordic and Baltic households could face higher electricity and heating bills.
cells.b: On January 26, 2026, the Council of the EU gave final approval to a regulation that ends Russian LNG imports from January 1, 2027, and pipeline gas imports by September 30, 2027. Finland and the three Baltic states have already cut themselves off from Russian gas and electricity, but they still feel price swings in Europe's integrated market. No effect on household bills in 2026 could be confirmed.

cells.m: The war, sanctions on Russia, and the EU's phased ban on Russian gas imports → Swings in European gas prices → Households in countries that rely heavily on gas imports, such as Italy and Greece, could face higher electricity and heating bills.
cells.b: On January 26, 2026, the Council of the EU gave final approval to a regulation that ends Russian LNG imports from January 1, 2027, and pipeline gas imports by September 30, 2027. After the war began in 2022, the surge in European gas prices was passed through to electricity bills in Southern Europe, but no effect on 2026 bills could be confirmed.

cells.m: Damage to the Druzhba pipeline and halted oil flows during the war → Disrupted crude supplies to Hungary and Slovakia, which depend on Russian oil → Fuel supplies and prices could become unstable.
cells.b: Ukraine's foreign minister said a Russian strike on January 27, 2026, had damaged the Ukrainian section of the Druzhba pipeline, and in February 2026 flows of Russian crude to Hungary and Slovakia stopped (The Moscow Times, citing Bloomberg). No effect on consumer prices could be confirmed. A separate gas price pathway to Germany and the rest of Western Europe remains.

cells.m: Each side strikes the other's energy facilities → Refinery shutdowns and power outages → Disrupted fuel and electricity supplies
cells.b: As reported on September 25, 2026, Ukrainian drone attacks shut down Russia's Novoshakhtinsk refinery and also hit refineries in Moscow and Yaroslavl.

cells.m: Continuing sanctions on Russia → South Korean companies cut production in Russia and exports to it → Lower revenue and fewer jobs at the companies involved
cells.b: According to an October 8, 2026, report citing South Korea's Foreign Ministry, South Korean exports to Russia fell from $10 billion in 2021 to $4 billion in 2025; exports of strategic goods are banned outright, and 1,402 non-strategic items require individual licenses. Hyundai Motor said in December 2025 that it could not buy back its stake in its St. Petersburg plant as long as the war continues, in effect giving up a buyback option due to expire in January 2026 (the 2024 sale cost it 287 billion won). No figures on employment changes at the companies involved could be confirmed.

cells.r: Russia accounts for a small share of U.S. trade, so the effect on Americans' daily lives through this channel is negligible.

cells.m: Sanctions on Russia and severed trade → Ports, logistics firms, and exporters in Finland and the Baltic states that relied on Russian cargo and on exports to Russia could keep losing income.
cells.b: According to a January 20, 2026, report, Latvian rail freight fell 17.6 percent to 9.4 million tons in 2025, less than a fifth of the 2015 level (55.6 million tons), and port-bound freight fell 29.3 percent. The state must spend up to 100 million euros a year to keep the railway running and has already put 26 million euros toward covering its 2024 losses. The industry blames the end of Russia-Europe transshipment after the 2022 invasion. Figures for Finland, Estonia, and Lithuania for 2026 could not be confirmed. Losses in Finland's eastern border region from the border closure are covered in the Population movement cell of the Baltic Sea and Kaliningrad flashpoint.

cells.r: Southern Europe's trade with Russia and Ukraine is small, so the effect on daily life through this channel is negligible.

cells.m: Sanctions on Russia, the loss of the Russian market, and an influx of Ukrainian farm products → Lower exports to Russia by manufacturers in Germany and elsewhere, and pressure on the incomes of farmers in Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia
cells.b: According to a March 10, 2026, report citing Germany's Federal Statistical Office, German exports to Russia in January 2026 were 514 million euros, down 15.9 percent from a year earlier. After the revised EU-Ukraine free trade agreement took effect on October 29, 2025, Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia kept their unilateral bans on Ukrainian farm imports, and the European Commission called on October 31 for the bans to be lifted. No figures on income changes for farmers in Central and Eastern Europe could be confirmed. The Central and Eastern European farm pathway was added when the definition of this population was broadened.

cells.m: Industrial shutdowns from airstrikes, and sanctions on Russia → Lower output and exports in both countries → Job and income losses
cells.b: As reported on September 25, 2026, ArcelorMittal halted production at Ukraine's largest steelworks after four strikes in five weeks killed five workers.

cells.r: Data such as government statements on cyberattacks or influence operations against South Korea linked to this war would settle this.
